extracted.intended_audience: readers of entertainment/celebrity news and the general public interested in TV industry developments
extracted.subtask_description: An entertainment news article presenting a public apology/transcript from a showrunner (Dan Harmon) and the accuser's public response (Megan Ganz). It frames the apology, recounts the incident in narrative form, and includes the full podcast transcript for readers to judge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think about it
rubrics_metrics.description: “Think about it. No matter who you are at work, no matter where you’re working... just think about it.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmon's repeated injunction that people in any workplace should consciously consider the consequences of their feelings and actions; not thinking lets people 'get away with not thinking about it' and cause technically legal but harmful damage. He frames cultural change as normalizing thinking and talking about such conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest in apology and acknowledge harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Apologies should go beyond 'I'm sorry' to explicitly acknowledge what was done and the harms caused.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmon says, “in addition to obviously being sorry... I did it by not thinking about it,” and enumerates concrete harms: "I lost my job. I ruined my show. I betrayed the audience. I destroyed everything, and I damaged her internal compass." The article also highlights that Ganz accepted public forgiveness to validate vindication rather than private resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not act on attraction to someone you have power over
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid pursuing romantic/sexual interest in an employee or anyone over whom you have professional power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmon: “I was attracted to a writer that I had power over because I was a showrunner... these feelings were bad news.” He admits failing to manage those feelings and that failing harmed others by undermining trust and professionalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not abuse positional power or mentorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Those in mentorship or supervisory roles must not use that position to control, manipulate, or punish subordinates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmon acknowledges he was "the one writing her paychecks and in control of whether she stayed or went" and that he used that influence to treat her cruelly and to try to 'teach her a lesson.' The article frames this as an abuse of mentor/professional power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making people doubt their competence/integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavior that causes an employee to question their ability or integrity is harmful and unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted: the targeted writer said focusing on her made her 'unable to know whether I’m good at my job.' Harmon recognizes that his attention undercut her faith in her talent and the production's faith in his judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public forgiveness/validation should be visible when appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: When misconduct is raised publicly, forgiveness or vindication may need to occur publicly to validate the accuser's experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Megan Ganz: “This was never about vengeance; it’s about vindication... if any part of this process should be done in the light, it’s the forgiveness part.” The article presents her public forgiveness as a deliberate, transparent act rather than a private settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge cultural/systemic dimensions, not just personal feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressing misconduct requires recognizing the broader culture that allows or normalizes harmful behavior, not merely describing private emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmon remarks on 'a culture of feeling things that you think are unique and significant' and frames his attraction and conduct within systemic problems—implying accountability includes cultural awareness and change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not gaslight or blame those who call out behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Responding to criticism by labeling observers as 'sexist' or 'jealous' is an anti-pattern that shifts blame away from the perpetrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmon admits he told others that if they found his behavior 'creepy or flirty or unprofessional,' then 'you were the sexist. You were jealous,' demonstrating an example of how perpetrators deflect responsibility and why that is wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept consequences and commit to not repeating the behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: Accountability includes accepting professional and personal consequences and a genuine commitment to change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmon notes consequences—losing his job and show—and states, 'I never did it before, and I will never do it again,' indicating acceptance of outcomes and a pledge to refrain from repeating the misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide full disclosure and allow public judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: When addressing public allegations, offering a full account and inviting others to examine it allows external judgment rather than a controlled private narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harmon: 'I want you to be the one to examine this every step of the way... I don't want to explain to you what I've learned. I want you to look at this and I want it to sound relatively unremarkable to you.' The article includes the full transcript to let readers assess for themselves.
